questions.q: Which table does vw_support_ticket_trends read from?
options: raw.tickets_stream, the Stream directly
raw.tickets_api_raw, the raw JSON table
marts.refund_events, the append-only table
marts.ticket_facts, the current-state table
questions.explain: Support's trend view reads from ticket_facts, the upserted current-state table kept in sync by ticket_facts_sync_task.

questions.q: Why doesn't vw_support_open_tickets need a window function to find each ticket's current status?
options: Window functions aren't supported in Snowflake views
Status values never change once a ticket is created
ticket_facts only ever holds one latest row per ticket, so a plain WHERE clause already reflects current state
It actually does need one, and this lesson is simplifying incorrectly
questions.explain: Because ticket_facts is a current-state (upserted) table, there's no need to deduplicate or find the 'latest' row — there's only ever one row per ticket.

questions.q: What three dimensions does vw_support_ticket_trends group by?
options: Ticket ID, loaded_at, and warehouse
Week, category, and priority
Only week, with no other grouping
Subscriber, refund amount, and status
questions.explain: The trend view groups by DATE_TRUNC('week', opened_at), category, and priority — the dimensions Support actually filters and slices by.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is true about vw_support_ticket_trends and vw_finance_refunds, despite looking like unrelated pipelines?
options: Both ultimately trace back to the exact same source: the same raw JSON flowing through the same tickets_stream
They share no common ancestry and are coincidentally similar in naming only
They are built from two entirely separate, independently-loaded copies of ticket data
One is built in Snowflake and the other is built entirely inside Power BI
questions.explain: Both views trace back to the same shared root — tickets_api_raw via tickets_stream — which is exactly why the two teams have every right to expect their numbers to reconcile.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the problem has to live in the shared pipeline, not in either view's own SQL, if Support and Finance's numbers ever disagree unexpectedly?
options: Because both views trace back to one shared upstream source, a real disagreement means something upstream of both views is inconsistent
Because Power BI always recalculates views correctly regardless of their SQL
Because Snowflake views cannot contain bugs by design
It doesn't say this — each view's SQL could independently be wrong instead
questions.explain: Given one shared root, an unexpected disagreement points at the shared pipeline (Streams/Tasks) rather than either view's own aggregation logic.
